strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: semantic segmentation when relevant class names are unknown at inference time. Automatically supplying names to an existing open-vocabulary segmentor could reduce manual prompting.

Decoding clustered BLIP patch embeddings into local captions is a useful methodological idea. The framework reuses pretrained components without additional fine-tuning and can conceptually support different segmentation backbones.

Table 1 provides encouraging evidence across three datasets: replacing plain BLIP captions with the proposed method improves cmIoU from 38.0 to 41.9 on VOC, 26.7 to 29.2 on ADE20K, and 29.2 to 35.8 on CityScapes.

The pipeline is generally understandable, principal models and datasets are attributed, and implementation parameters and evaluator prompts are supplied. Appendix B usefully documents hallucinated names, overly generic descriptions, and competition between related labels.
weaknesses: The central evaluation method, LOVE, is insufficiently validated. Appendix A instructs the LLM to map stuff categories to background even for ADE20K and CityScapes, which evaluate such categories; the exact-name override only partly mitigates this problem. ADE20K mapping also relies on the LLM recalling the dataset vocabulary rather than receiving its 847 classes. No human-validated mapping accuracy, quantitative comparison with alternative mappers, or prompt-sensitivity study establishes that the resulting mIoU reliably measures semantic correctness.

The state-of-the-art comparison is not adequately controlled. Table 2 reports 41.6 versus 20.1 mIoU against ZeroSeg on VOC, but does not establish a shared label-mapping protocol or account for differences in pretrained components and supervision. No competing automatic-class method is reported on ADE20K or CityScapes. These results therefore provide weaker support for the superiority claims than the text suggests.

The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the class-discovery contribution. Table 1 uses class-agnostic matching, which ignores naming errors and does not directly penalize unmatched predicted segments. The simple BLIP-plus-X-Decoder baseline should also receive semantic mIoU evaluation under the same mapper and comparable caption-generation budget. Separate ablations of multiscale clustering, alignment, positional features, and denoising are missing, leaving their necessity unclear.

The model-selection protocol leaves uncertainty about generalization. Section 4.1 reports Bayesian optimization against VOC mIoU without identifying a disjoint tuning split, while Table 2 uses the best dataset-specific caption counts from Table 3. The manuscript should establish separation between tuning and final evaluation. Repeated-run variability is also absent despite stochastic clustering and caption generation.

Some reproducibility and practical details remain unresolved. Section 3.1 describes Hungarian matching, whereas Equation 10 specifies independent maximum-IoU assignments; these are different procedures. Alignment between the two patch-grid resolutions also needs clarification. Runtime and memory measurements are missing despite using up to twenty captioning cycles in the headline results. These issues are secondary to the evaluation concerns but limit assessment of practical impact.
